application_type: single-clip video question answering over egocentric robot manipulation footage -- Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct on one GB200, the video counterpart to the multi-image bundles on this tray
daily_active_users_u_reason: (U) this campaign was specified directly in concurrent users, not DAU
peak_to_mean_u_reason: (U) not applicable; CCU is already the peak figure
requests_per_session_u_reason: (U) the ladder issues independent requests rather than multi-turn sessions, so no per-session request count was declared
image_resolution_mix_u_reason: (U) no image is sent; this corpus is video only. The resolution that does drive cost in this run is the video frame resolution, and the schema has no field for it -- see the note on where the video resolution mix had to go.
video_sampling_fps_u_reason: (U) the application specifies a frame budget, not a rate: every clip is summarized in 16 frames regardless of length, so there is no fps the application requires. video_max_frames carries the requirement, and it matches the delivered value in serving.media_preprocessing exactly. An application that instead required fixed temporal resolution -- 1 frame per second of footage, say -- would give this field a value and would make context length grow with clip duration, which under this policy it does not.
reasoning_share_u_reason: (U) reasoning_share is meaningful only for a mixed workload; no record in this corpus carries a reasoning turn, so the run is uniformly non-thinking

notes.every_media_figure_here_is_corpus_exact_: The three multi-image bundles on this tray declared their media term from a few hundred sampled draws. This one did not have to: the corpus is 1,000 records, and all 1,000 were sent to the live server and priced, with zero errors. media_tokens_per_request 5,798.73 is therefore the exact mean over the whole population the ladder draws from, not an estimate of it, and the run's own prompt-token total is a check on nothing but the sampler. The measurement sent each record twice, once with the video part and once with the text part alone, so the difference is the server's own media cost with the chat template held constant -- the same method the multi-image campaign used, applied to every record instead of a sample.
notes.the_media_cost_is_exactly_bimodal_and_th: There are two resolutions in this corpus and only two. 633 clips are 960x768 and every one of them costs exactly 7,346 media tokens. 367 clips are 640x480 and every one costs exactly 3,130. Not approximately: the within-group variance is zero across all 1,000 measurements. The mean of 5,798.73 is 0.633 x 7,346 + 0.367 x 3,130, and it describes no clip in the corpus -- no request costs anything close to 5,798 tokens. This is the sharpest available demonstration of why ASCEP prefers a declared mix to a declared mean. A reader sizing KV from the mean is sizing for a request that does not exist, and relative to that mean the true costs are plus 26.7 percent for the 7,346-token majority and minus 46.0 percent for the 3,130-token minority, so a reader sizing from it under-provisions the common case and over-provisions the rare one.
notes.the_video_resolution_mix_has_nowhere_to_: image_resolution_mix exists and is the schema's answer to a mean hiding a spread; there is no video_resolution_mix. On this workload the frame resolution is the whole cost story -- it is the only thing separating a 7,346-token request from a 3,130-token one -- and the only place it can be declared is prose. The mix, for the record, is 960x768 at fraction 0.633 and 640x480 at fraction 0.367, summing to 1.000. That completeness is itself worth noting: both multi-image campaigns declared truncated mixes covering under 5 percent of their images, because almost every image had its own resolution. Here the mix is exhaustive and would have been trivial to validate against the SHOULD-sum-to-1 rule, if the field existed. Recorded as a gap rather than patched by inventing a field in an example, the same precedent the earlier bundles set.
notes.video_seconds_per_request_is_declared_bu: 66.521 s is the measured mean clip duration, over a range of 11.233 to 240.400 s, and the corpus totals 66,521.1 s of footage. The schema pairs this field with video_sampling_fps to derive a frame count, and under a rate-based policy it would be a first-order cost driver. Under this deployment's uniform-count policy it drives nothing: the 240 s clip and the 11 s clip cost identical vision tokens. It is declared anyway, and honestly rather than as a formality, because it is a first-order driver of host CPU -- at 30 fps native the mean request has roughly 1,996 frames demuxed and decoded so that 16 can be kept -- and because a reader who changes the frame policy needs it to recompute the media term.
notes.the_effective_sampling_rate_and_why_it_i: Dividing 16 frames by each clip's duration gives the rate the clip was effectively sampled at: minimum 0.0666 fps on the 240.4 s clip, median 0.2780, mean 0.3207, maximum 1.4243 fps on the 11.2 s clip. That is a 21.4-fold spread in temporal resolution across one corpus under one unchanged policy, and it is a real property of the workload with real consequences for answer quality -- the longest clips are summarized at one frame every 15 s. It is not video_sampling_fps in either schema, because both of those fields mean a chosen rate and no rate was chosen here. It sits in prose because the protocol has no field for a realized-rate distribution, which is the second gap this campaign found in the video half of the schema.
notes.input_tokens_per_request_is_much_larger_: 540.42 tokens is the measured mean server-reported prompt_tokens for the text part alone, chat template included, over all 1,000 records, ranging 524 to 662. The multi-image campaigns on this tray declared 39.5 and 33.5 for the same field. The gap is the corpus, not the model: these records carry long structured task descriptions of a robot manipulation episode, where the image corpus carried short questions. It is worth flagging because it changes the shape of the workload. Media is 91.5 percent of the mean prompt here, against 99.1 percent in the Qwen multi-image bundle, so this is the one media campaign on this tray where the text term is not a rounding error and a reader cannot approximate the prompt by the media term alone.
notes.avg_context_tokens_composition: 6,589.15 is 540.42 text plus 5,798.73 media plus half of the 500 output tokens, tagged M because both prompt terms are server-measured over the entire corpus. The measured full-prompt mean is 6,339.15, which is exactly the sum of the two prompt terms, so the M covers them jointly and not just individually. The 250-token output half is the residency convention every ASCEP report uses -- a request holds its generated tokens for on average half the generation -- and is a model, not a measurement; it is stated here so a reader does not read the M as covering all three terms. Prompt length ranges 3,654 to 8,008 tokens, which with 500 output tokens fits inside the 32,768-token max_model_len with a wide margin, so no request in this campaign was truncated or refused for length.
notes.the_corpus_was_truncated_to_1000_records: The source split holds 2,000 records. It was cut to the first 1,000 so the base64-inlined media would sit in host RAM for the whole run at about 5.84 GB, or 5.44 GiB, which is what makes the arrival times mean anything. The full 2,000 would also have fit, so the cut bounds build time and resident footprint rather than working around a RAM limit; see the hardware note. The cut is by position, not by sampling, so it inherits whatever ordering the source split has, and the 0.633 / 0.367 resolution split is a property of those first 1,000 records rather than a claim about the full dataset. A reader reproducing this bundle against the whole split may get a different mix and therefore a different media mean, and would need to re-measure rather than reuse 5,798.73.
notes.concurrent_users_and_duty_cycle_are_inhe: 200 users at a 0.25 duty cycle and 15 tokens per second per user are carried over unchanged from both multi-image campaigns on this tray, so that the three bundles differ only in modality and in what the media costs. They describe a hypothetical deployment and nothing in the ladder measures them; the 750 tok/s demand exists to be compared against measured capacity, and on this workload the comparison is not close. Retaining them across modalities is the point: it is what lets a reader ask how many GPUs the same 750 tok/s service needs as it moves from text to images to video.
notes.the_ladder_and_the_gates_are_not_inherit: The ladder is concurrency 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 32 with 3 repetitions, 120 s windows, 500 output tokens with ignore_eos and 1.5 s think time. It is much lower and much finer than the 4-to-128 ladder both multi-image campaigns used, because a placement probe run before the ladder -- four rungs, 45 s each, reported in the README -- put the interesting region in single digits, and a ladder whose first rung already fails measures nothing. The SLO gates were fixed before that probe and were not moved by it: ttft_p95 4.0 s, itl_p95 0.0667 s, e2e_p95 120 s, error cap 1.0 percent. The ttft gate is the one that differs from the sibling campaigns' 2.5 s, and it is raised on an application argument, not a results argument: a user who has just submitted a 58-second clip is waiting on a video to be ingested and understood, not on a chat reply, and 2.5 s is a chat number. The other three gates are unchanged, so latency-per-token and error tolerance stay directly comparable across all three bundles.
notes.the_corpus_is_pinned_by_digest_because_i: corpus.jsonl is 1,000 records and sha256 340b10426a6a9e693736152b19c446b61ae865d9da03fa6cfc6214ba1339455e over the record file, against 4,381,298,125 bytes of third-party MP4 under media/ that this repository does not republish. Neither the record file nor the footage ships in the bundle, so this digest is the only thing binding the published figures to a specific corpus: a reader who obtains the same clips can confirm they hold the same 1,000 records in the same order before comparing any number here, and can tell a genuine disagreement from a different corpus. No earlier campaign in this directory pinned its corpus this way, and each of them should have -- a media bundle whose media is unpublishable is otherwise reproducible only in outline.
